title: Mio, My Son
author: Astrid Lindgren
short_summary: Bo Vilhelm Olsson — Bosse — is nine years old and lives in Stockholm with an elderly couple who do not like boys and tell him to keep out of the way. One evening a kind shopkeeper gives him an apple and asks him to post a card, the apple turns to gold in his hands, and a spirit in a bottle carries him away to Farawayland, where a king is waiting who calls him Mio, my Mio. But there is a knight with a heart of stone in the land beyond, and he has been taking children.
extended_summary:
Bosse is a foster child. His mother died when he was born, his foster parents complain about him to the neighbours, and his one friend is a boy called Benke. On his way home one evening, Mrs. Lundin at the fruit stall gives him an apple and asks him to post a card for her. The card is addressed to a king and says that his son is coming home, and will be known by the golden apple he carries — and when Bosse looks again, the apple in his hand is gold. He frees a spirit from a bottle in the park, and the spirit, seeing the apple, carries him off over the roofs.

In Farawayland his father the king knows him at once and calls him Mio. He is given a horse with a golden mane, Miramis, and a best friend, Jum-Jum, and for a while there is nothing but roses, bread that satisfies hunger and evenings of music. But everyone speaks in whispers about the land beyond the mountains, where the knight Sir Kato — whose heart is made of stone — has been carrying children away, and the story has been waiting for Mio all along.

Mio and Jum-Jum go, knowing what it means. The book never settles whether any of this is true: it begins with a boy alone on a park bench in Stockholm and ends with Mio saying that he is in Farawayland and that his father the king is with him — and leaves the reader to decide what to do with that.

questions.prompt: On his way home, Bosse is given something by Mrs. Lundin at the fruit stall, and asked to do something for her. What are they?

options: An apple, and a card she wants posted
A coin, and a message for the baker
A bottle, and a bag to carry home
A pear, and a letter for his foster parents

questions.explanation: Two small kindnesses from a shopkeeper who has noticed that nobody else is kind to him. Everything in the book follows from that apple and that card, and Mrs. Lundin never explains herself — she simply seems to know.

questions.prompt: Bosse reads the card he has been asked to post. What does it say?

options: That the king's son is coming, known by a golden apple
That a boy in the city is in danger and must be fetched
That the roses in Farawayland have begun to die
That a knight with a stone heart is stealing children

questions.explanation: He is holding an ordinary apple when he reads it. By the time he looks down again, the apple is gold — and the card in his hand has just told him who he is, several minutes before he understands it.

questions.prompt: In Farawayland the boy learns that Bosse was never his real name. His father the king calls him ___.
questions.explanation: The phrase "Mio, my Mio" runs through the whole book, and it is the thing Bosse most wants in the world: not a kingdom or a horse, but somebody who says his name as though it mattered.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the horse Mio's father gives him?

options: Miramis
Melisant
Morando
Mirabell

questions.explanation: A white horse with a golden mane, who can gallop over the sky. Lindgren gives Mio everything a lonely child would ask for — a father, a friend, a horse — before she tells him what he will have to do with it.

questions.prompt: Put the beginning of Mio's story in the order it happens.

items: Bosse sits alone on a bench in a Stockholm park
Mrs. Lundin gives him an apple and a card to post
The apple in his hand turns to gold
A spirit is let out of a bottle in the park
The king in Farawayland calls him Mio, my Mio
Mio and Jum-Jum set out for the land beyond

questions.explanation: The transformation happens in four quiet steps, all of them in an ordinary Stockholm evening: a bench, a shop, an apple, a bottle. Lindgren spends only a few pages on the real world, and every one of them matters.

questions.prompt: Match each person or creature to who they are in Mio's story.

right: The one friend Bosse had in Stockholm
The shopkeeper who hands over the apple
The best friend Mio finds in Farawayland
The horse with the golden mane

questions.explanation: Notice the pairing: Bosse had one friend in the real world and gets one friend in the other, and the only adult who was ever kind to him is the one who sends him. Farawayland is not the opposite of Stockholm — it is Stockholm's few good things, made larger.

questions.prompt: Sort each detail by which of the boy's two lives it belongs to.

options.label: Being told to keep out of the way at home
Sitting on a park bench with nowhere to go
One friend, and nobody else who notices him
A father who says his name over and over
A horse with a golden mane to ride
A friend who comes with him into danger

questions.explanation: Every item on the right answers an item on the left, one for one. That exactness is why readers argue about the ending: Farawayland gives Bosse precisely what he is missing, in precisely the order he is missing it.

questions.prompt: Sir Kato is described again and again in the same way. What is his heart made of?

options: Stone
Iron
Ice
Glass

questions.explanation: A heart of stone, repeated until it stops being a figure of speech and becomes a fact about his body. Lindgren's villain is frightening not because he is powerful but because there is nothing inside him that can be reached.

questions.prompt: The book begins with a lonely boy on a park bench in Stockholm, and ends with Mio saying he is in Farawayland with his father the king. Do you think Farawayland is really happening, or is Bosse still on that bench? Give your reasons — and say what difference your answer makes.
questions.explanation: There is no right answer and the book refuses to settle it. A strong answer gives evidence for its reading — the golden apple and the spirit on one side, the exactness with which Farawayland supplies what Bosse lacks on the other — and then does the harder part: says whether it matters. The best answers notice that the boy is happy in both readings, and that this is uncomfortable.

questions.prompt: Farawayland has places with names like the Land Outside and the island in the Sea of Morning. Invent one more place for Mio to ride Miramis to: what is it called, what would he see there, and would it be a good place or a frightening one?
questions.explanation: There is no single right answer. A strong invention gives the place a name that sounds like Lindgren's — plain words put together strangely — and describes one concrete thing you would see. Saying whether it is beautiful or frightening is part of the task: in this book the two are often the same place.

questions.prompt: Before any of it begins, Bosse is nine years old and living with an elderly couple who tell him to keep out of the ___.
questions.explanation: It is the whole of his home life in one phrase, and Lindgren puts it near the front so that everything afterwards is measured against it. He is not beaten or starved; he is simply not wanted, which for a nine-year-old is quite enough.

questions.prompt: Why is everyone in Farawayland afraid of the land beyond the mountains?

options: Sir Kato has been carrying children away from the villages
The bridge across the border has fallen into the sea
Nobody who rides there can find the way back home
The king has forbidden anyone to cross the border

questions.explanation: The children are taken and do not come back, and the whole country speaks about it in whispers. It is also why the story cannot end with Mio simply being happy: he is the one person the missing children are waiting for.
